issues.legal_issue: The executing court’s role in an execution sale continues to include proceedings to obtain possession of the property.
material_facts: A money decree was enforced through the court-supervised sale of immovable property.
After the sale, the purchaser paid the balance and a conveyance was executed on behalf of the judgment-debtors.
The purchaser sought vacant possession through the executing court rather than by filing a separate suit.
issues.conclusion: The execution proceedings do not end with the sale or execution of the conveyance insofar as possession remains to be obtained; the purchaser may seek possession through the executing court under Order XXI, Rules 95 and 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXI, Rules 95 to 102 of the Code of Civil Procedure place applications for possession after an execution sale within the sequence of execution proceedings. The Court agreed with Kailash Chandra Tarafdar v. Gopal Chandra Poddar that the executing court’s duty does not necessarily end upon confirmation of the sale.

predicates.execution_sale_possession_request: A purchaser sought possession of immovable property sold through proceedings to enforce a decree.
predicates.sale_conveyance_completed: A conveyance of the property was executed for the purchaser after the court-supervised sale.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks possession after a conveyance following an execution sale, the execution proceedings continue to address possession.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute over possession between a judgment-debtor and a purchaser at an execution sale is for the executing court when it concerns the rights purchased or resistance to delivery.
material_facts: The purchaser sought vacant possession of the property sold in execution of a decree.
The judgment-debtors were asked to deliver the portion they occupied, and the application for possession was contested on the ground that the purchaser would need to bring a separate suit.
The dispute concerned delivery of the property and the rights acquired at the execution sale.
issues.conclusion: The dispute is one relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree and must be determined by the executing court, not in a separate suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure is to be construed liberally. A purchaser at a sale in execution is a party for the purposes of that section, whether or not the purchaser is the decree-holder; questions between the purchaser and the judgment-debtor concerning the rights purchased or resistance to delivery therefore fall within the executing court’s jurisdiction. The Court followed Kailash Chandra Tarafdar v. Gopal Chandra Poddar, relied on the Privy Council’s reasoning in Prosunno Coomar Sanyal v. Kalidas Sanyal and Ganapathy v. Krishnamachariar, and overruled Ram Singh Gopal Singh v. Abdullah Habibullah.

predicates.execution_sale_possession_dispute: A dispute arose in proceedings to enforce a decree after immovable property was sold to a purchaser.
predicates.judgment_debtor_contests_delivery: The judgment-debtor resisted or contested delivery of the property to the purchaser.
predicates.dispute_concerns_purchased_rights: The dispute concerned the rights acquired by the purchaser or the delivery of the property sold.

issues.definition: When a judgment-debtor contests delivery in a dispute arising from an execution sale and the dispute concerns the rights purchased, the dispute is determined in the execution proceeding.
